newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire tries to stop Tutsi exodus, governor defiant.
newsitem.headline: Zaire tries to stop Tutsi exodus, governor defiant.

text.p: Zaire suspended the regional administrator who ordered ethnic Tutsis to leave the country but it was unclear on Monday if this would halt a Tutsi exodus.
South Kivu Deputy Governor Lwasi Ngabo Lwabanji who gave some 200,000 Tutsis or Banyamulenges a week to leave, expiring on Tuesday, said he was told by telephone he had been suspended.
"I am still waiting for a formal recall to the capital," he told Reuters by telephone from the provincial capital Bukavu.

But signalling that he might be backed by local army units embroiled in fighting with the Tutsis, Lwabanja said he was consulting the military on how to proceed with expulsions. He said a decision would be made on Wednesday or Thursday.
Military and civilian authorities in Kinshasa mainatin there is no quit order to Tutsis, but the government's hold on provinces of the vast Central African nation is known to be tenuous.

"I know of no operation against the Banyamulenge people as a whole, but certainly the Zairean army will continue operations against those of them who have taken up arms," government spokesman Boguo Makeli said.
It is not clear if the government has control of military operations against Banyamulenge, who settled in the region about 200 years ago from Rwanda.

Strongman President Mobutu Sese Seko who has held the country of about 45 million diverse people together during more than 30 years in power, has been convalescing in Europe since undergoing prostrate surgery in August. His powerful Interior Minister Kamanda wa Kamanda is also abroad, while Prime Minister Kengo wa Dendo has also been in and out of the country recently.

Asked if Kinshasa had taken measures to ensure neither soldiers nor members of the local indigenous population did not chase out Tutsis abitrarily, a senior government official admitted the situatioin was becoming more difficult to control.
The official, who asked not to be identified, said the Banyamulenge had made a grave mistake by taking up arms against the Zairean army, fuelling tension in an already tense region.

"Traditionally the Banyamulenge Tutsis are dynamic and wealthy so there is a tendency among other groups to recent them," he said. "By taking up arms the Banyamulenge are paving the way for other communities to chase them away."
The official added that indigenous Zaireans had volunteered to help the army in battling Banyamulenge rebels.

Aid workers say they fear all-out war in the sub-region because of the quit order. The Rwanda army, which is dominated by Tutsis, has exchanged fire with Zairean troops and the Burundi army, also predominnatly Tutsi, risks being drawn in.
Clashes between Banyamulenges and indigenous peoples have degenerated into virtual civil war since more than a million rival Rwanda Hutus fled violence into the same region in 1994.
